Experiment debug report

Debugging exp_003_4: why the action predictor never learns

A self-reinforcing curiosity loop drives the policy into walls — and the architecture quietly tells us so through its gradients before we ever look at the agent.
Single-page analysis · LS20 Level 1 · JEPA world-model + dual predictor · 500k steps · 2026-05-13

Context — what exp_003_4 is

The project. A JEPA-style world model trained on screen frames of the ARC-AGI-3 game LS20 Level 1 (a 64×64 grid puzzle, 4 directional actions). The world model produces a 4-latent reasoning state Ht ∈ ℝ4×128 from each frame via a patch-SA encoder feeding a Perceiver resampler. The policy reads Ht and outputs an action; the agent is rewarded with curiosity, not external rewards.

What is special about exp_003_4. It is identical to exp_003_2 except the Perceiver resampler no longer does self-attention among its 4 latents within each round — every round is now cross-attention only. The hypothesis being tested is whether SA-among-latents is load-bearing for representational diversity, or merely redundant on top of cross-attention.

How collapse is meant to be prevented. No EMA target encoder. Instead, an action predictor reads the pair (Ht, Ht+1) and is trained to recover the action at by cross-entropy. The information-theoretic argument: if the encoder collapses (Ht≈Ht+1), then no classifier can recover the action and Laction saturates at ln 4. Gradients from Laction back through the encoder therefore push it to keep adjacent latents action-discriminative.

Joint loss & rewards (both 0.5/0.5).

L_total = 0.5 · L_state  +  0.5 · L_action            (encoder update)
r_t     = clamp(0.5 · MSE(ĥ_{t+1}, h_{t+1})
              + 0.5 · CE(p_pred, a_t), 50)            (intrinsic reward)

That second equation will turn out to be where the trouble lives.

Run snapshot — what 500K steps produced

So the story we already see at a glance: the world model learned to predict next-state well, the action half never finished, and most of the policy's curiosity reward in late training comes from one place — action ambiguity. Keep that in mind as we step through the six odd things in the gradient panel.

Obs #1 — eff rank ↑ to ≈2 but pairwise cosine stays ≈0.9

Is the observation real?

Yes — both numbers are correct, and they are not in conflict.

Mechanism — how rank can grow while cosine stays high

Effective rank is computed on the centred latent matrix (singular values of H − μ), while pairwise cosine similarity is computed on the raw latents. The two measure orthogonal things:

  • Eff rank ≈ 2 means the 4 latents span a 2-D subspace once you subtract their common mean. They are no longer parallel — they fan out into a plane.
  • Pairwise cos ≈ 0.9 means the four vectors are still tightly clustered around a single direction — small angular spread.

Picture four arrows that all point roughly toward the same hemisphere, but differ slightly: their pairwise dot products (after norming) are large (≈0.9) because they share most of their direction, yet a PCA of the cloud reveals a 2-D structure. That is exactly the regime exp_003_4 has settled into.

Why this matters in this experiment

The dashboard's "collapse" alarm uses cosine; the recovery signal uses rank. Here they disagree, because partial de-collapse along one anti-correlated axis can fan two of the four latents apart without dropping the global cosine much. The round0_postSA_pairwise_cossim probe (still ≈0.94 at the end) tells us cross-attention R0 is producing four nearly-identical token reads — the spread that does develop happens further downstream (R1 + output_norm).

Implication

The action predictor's grip on encoder collapse is mostly working — but only weakly. The four latents are still co-linear enough that they encode roughly one direction's worth of information about the frame. Compare to the in-rollout t=10/t=20 series, which never escapes 0.998 — when the recurrent state is allowed to settle, the four queries re-cluster.

Obs #2 — patch-SA: cos(gaction,Ht, gaction,Ht+1) is always strongly negative

What's being measured

The action predictor reads the pair (Ht, Ht+1). By rerunning torch.autograd.grad twice with the other endpoint detached, the monitor decomposes the gradient flowing into every upstream module into two parts: one that came via the Ht input, and one that came via the Ht+1 input. The cosine of those two flattened gradient vectors tells us whether the action loss pulls the same parameter in the same direction through both input paths (positive), in unrelated directions (≈0), or against itself (negative).

Mechanism — why patch-SA gets the cancellation

The encoder is called twice per training step on different frames:

h_t_fresh   = encoder(frame_t,   h_queries.detach())     # forward 1
h_tp1_fresh = encoder(frame_{t+1}, h_t_fresh.detach())   # forward 2

The patch-SA stack (color_embed → patch_proj → 2 SA blocks → sa_norm) is a pure function of the frame; it does not see the recurrent query at all. So the same parameters process two different frames in two distinct forward passes. Concatenate the two outputs [Ht, Ht+1] into the action predictor's MLP. The MLP can only recover the action from the difference between the two reads. By symmetry of cross-entropy, the gradient w.r.t. one read is approximately the negative of the gradient w.r.t. the other:

∂L_action/∂H_t   ≈ −∂L_action/∂H_{t+1}     (along the discriminative direction)

Because the same patch-SA parameters are reached by chain rule from both endpoints — and the two endpoints' gradient vectors point opposite ways in latent space — most of the contribution cancels at the parameter level once you sum them. The leftover (positive on a few dims, negative on others) is what gets clipped and applied.

Implications

  • Most of the action gradient on the patch encoder cancels itself. Even though gnorm_patch_sa_from_action_via_Ht and ..._Ht+1 are each ≈0.1–0.4 individually, their sum is much smaller. The patch encoder is therefore much harder for Laction to move than the raw per-source norms suggest.
  • This is not a bug, it's a property. Any parameter that is "shared" across the two input branches of a Siamese-style head will see anti-correlated gradients when the head's objective is a function of the difference. The asymmetric paths (Perceiver — see Obs #4) get a much cleaner signal.

Why the gradients cancel — concrete example

Consider a frame where action a=DOWN moves the player down by 1 row. The action predictor wants to increase the difference between Ht and Ht+1 along whatever direction encodes "player row". Pushing Ht up the direction and Ht+1 down it both increase the gap — and both come from the same patch-SA weights with opposite signs. Sum at the parameter → small net move.

Obs #3 — cos(gstate, gaction) ≈ 0 across all modules

From the same plot above (left panel): gcossim_state_vs_action hovers between −0.05 and +0.1 for every module group, all the time. The state and action losses pull each module in orthogonal directions.

Is "orthogonal" good or bad?

It's the in-between case. It tells us:

  • The two losses do not fight — they're not negative-cosine, so we're not in a tug-of-war where each step is wasted.
  • The two losses do not cooperate — they're not positive-cosine, so progress on one does not transfer to the other.

In the language of multi-task learning, the two heads have decoupled subspaces in the encoder's weight space. Mathematically that means we can decompose any encoder update into a "state-pred part" and an "action-pred part" and they live in different directions of θ.

What this implies for our problem

  • Driving Lstate to near-zero gives zero help to Laction. We can read that off the trajectory in the snapshot: Lstate drops 3 orders of magnitude while Laction moves by <1×.
  • The two losses share no representational target. The state predictor is content to learn a representation that just preserves enough of the frame to do flow matching; the action predictor needs a different representation (one that makes (Ht, Ht+1) action-separable). The encoder is being asked for two unrelated jobs, and is happy to grow two unrelated subspaces of features — see how eff rank stalls at ≈2.4 rather than reaching 4.

This is unlike the patch-SA pairwise-input cancellation in Obs #2, which is a real destructive interaction. Obs #3 is the milder failure: not fighting, but not helping either.

Obs #4 — Perceiver Cross-Attn R0: cos(gaction,Ht, gaction,Ht+1) ≈ 0

Same metric as Obs #2, different module. At perc_cross_r0 the cosine sits at ≈0 the whole run; at perc_cross_r1 it is moderately negative. Why does R0 behave differently from patch-SA?

Mechanism — different queries break the symmetry

R0 is the first Perceiver round. Its job is to attend from the latent queries to the 16 patch tokens. The two forward passes of the training step do not give R0 the same query:

forward 1:  R0 reads with queries = h_queries.detach()         # h_{t-1} from rollout
forward 2:  R0 reads with queries = h_t_fresh.detach()         # the just-encoded H_t

So R0 is processing two genuinely different (Q, K, V) inputs across the two encoder calls. The two gradient signals it receives — one via Ht, one via Ht+1 — are conditioned on independent input distributions. With nothing structurally tying them together (no shared input, no symmetric output target), their cosine averages to ≈0: they look like two independent random variables in parameter-gradient space.

R1 is closer to symmetric — it receives R0's output as its query in both cases — which is why its pairwise-input cosine sits at a mild −0.05 to −0.30: a residual ghost of the Obs-#2 cancellation, but weaker.

Implication

R0 is doing the most work of any module: it gets nearly twice the gradient power per step (because the two paths add nearly orthogonally rather than cancel) and its forward inputs vary the most across the two encoder calls. That sets us up for Obs #5.

Obs #5 — gnorm via Ht+1 on R0 grows without bound

Mechanism — why this specific gradient grows

Three forces interact:

  1. Lstate has been driven near zero. Its source norm into R0 grew because as the encoder learns, the upstream Jacobian becomes more aligned with informative directions — but the loss value is already small, so its contribution to the weight update is small in absolute terms.
  2. Laction is still ≈ 0.5 nats. Cross-entropy gradient magnitude scales with ‖p − y‖; at 0.5 nats we are still ≈ 30–40% wrong on average, so the upstream signal is strong.
  3. R0 is the asymmetric module (Obs #4). The Ht+1-path gradient doesn't have the Obs-#2 cancellation cousin to fight with, so it survives the chain back to R0's CA parameters intact.

Putting these together: Laction's gradient goes through the second encoder forward, which encodes frame_{t+1}, which is a different distribution than the first forward sees. R0 has to handle both. And because the second forward's gradient is the one with strong loss left to back-propagate, that gradient grows as the network gets better at not hitting cancellation on the Ht+1 path.

Why this is troubling

The other half of this experiment is the policy. Curiosity reward depends on the action predictor's residual error. If R0 is being shaped almost entirely by L_action via Ht+1, then R0 is being optimised to better encode the next frame's patches — exactly the thing the agent could trivially make pointless (Obs #6).

Obs #6 — why Laction never reaches zero: the wall-hitting loop

Everything above is mechanistic; the punchline is about the policy. Two debug episodes were rolled out — one early (step 5,000) and one late (step 500,000) — and the raw frames were inspected.

Quantifying "wall hit"

A "wall hit" is operationally defined as a step where the masked pixel diff between frame_t and frame_{t+1} is below 20 pixels (rows 61-62 zeroed because that is the always-changing step-counter display). The agent did move but nothing visible changed.

The mechanism in words

The agent is optimising intrinsic curiosity reward, which after the state predictor converged is dominated by the action term:

r_t  ≈  0.5 · CE(action_predictor(H_t, H_{t+1}),  a_t)

That term is large exactly when (Ht, Ht+1) does not let the predictor recover at. The cheapest way for the policy to make that happen is to render Ht and Ht+1 nearly identical — and the cheapest way to do that is to take an action that produces no observable frame change, i.e. hit a wall. The encoder is deterministic; identical input frames yield identical latents. So the policy has found a closed-form exploit:

The self-reinforcing curiosity loop

  1. Policy chooses action that walks into a wall.
  2. Frame doesn't change (modulo the masked counter strip).
  3. Encoder produces Ht ≈ Ht+1.
  4. Action predictor cannot recover at from an empty difference signal → high CE.
  5. High CE → high curiosity reward → REINFORCE reinforces step 1.

The action predictor cannot "learn its way out" because it is fundamentally being fed inputs that contain no signal. The encoder can't fix it either: there is nothing in the frames to encode. So Laction plateaus, and the policy specialises further into walls.

Why this connects to Obs #5

The L_action via Ht+1 gradient on R0 grows precisely because the encoder is being asked, again and again, to make Ht+1 just a little more distinguishable from Ht — but on inputs where the two frames are bit-identical. R0 absorbs an ever-larger gradient that cannot succeed at its task because there is no information to extract. The growing norm is the signature of an objective that the policy has poisoned at its source.

Corroborating per-class evidence

Reading right-to-left: the policy stops sampling the actions that would move it, the action predictor only sees the wall-pressing actions, and learns to predict UP vs DOWN (mostly chance from Ht≈Ht+1) while incidentally getting LEFT right when it happens to occur on a real move. The per-class plot is the gradient panel's story in object-level form.

Latent-trajectory drift confirms the policy is static, not exploring

For comparison — the early checkpoint

The contrast is the clearest piece of evidence we have: the wall-hitting strategy emerges as the action predictor improves. It is a strategy that becomes more valuable as the predictor gets better at non-wall steps, because the gap between wall-hit CE and moving-step CE grows. The policy is doing exactly what REINFORCE asked it to do; the reward function is what is wrong.

What to change

The findings above suggest a small set of pointed interventions, ordered from cheap to substantive.

  1. Stop rewarding action-predictor failure on near-static transitions. The cheapest fix: gate reward_w_action on the masked frame diff. If ‖frame_t − frame_{t+1}‖masked < ε, set the action component of the reward to zero. The agent then has no incentive to hit walls. (A cleaner version: subtract a baseline = the action-pred CE on a stationary buffer of (s, s) pairs, so only informative ambiguity is rewarded.)
  2. Penalise no-op transitions. Add a small constant negative reward when the masked frame diff is below a threshold. This pushes the policy away from walls regardless of what the predictor says.
  3. Use the policy-entropy bonus that is already in the config. policy_entropy_lambda = 0.10 is the right order of magnitude, but the policy still collapses — verify that the entropy term is in fact applied to the masked logits (the system card warns about this) and that no early-stopping is happening on entropy.
  4. Decouple curiosity from policy reward, or schedule it down. The state-component reward has effectively zero scale by step 100k; keeping the action component at full weight after that creates the exact bias that drives Obs #6. Linear decay of reward_w_action over training, or replacing it with an external task reward once the model is up, would both work.
  5. Look at the placeholder gradient path. drift-from-init = 1.0 for 500k steps is suspicious — the four placeholders are the only intra-latent diversity source now that SA-among-latents is removed (the change this experiment was actually designed to test). If their gradient is broken, the eff-rank ≈ 2 ceiling is partly an architectural artifact, not just a wall-hitting symptom.
  6. Reconsider whether the action predictor is the right anti-collapse regulariser at all. Its core assumption is that an action-determinable transition is a transition the encoder must keep informative. That assumption inverts when the policy can choose action-indeterminable transitions. EMA targets (as in exp_003_1) do not have this failure mode because they don't depend on the action being recoverable. A revisit of the SA-among-latents ablation should probably be carried out against EMA, not against the action predictor, to isolate the architectural effect this experiment was originally about.

One-line summary

The action predictor's training signal turned into a free reward the policy could exploit by pressing into walls; the gradient panel quietly tells us this in three places — Obs #2 (patch-SA cancellation), Obs #4 (R0 asymmetry), and Obs #5 (the Ht+1-path norm that grows without delivering a falling loss). The cosine-vs-rank split in Obs #1 is real but innocuous; the orthogonality in Obs #3 is a missed opportunity rather than a fight. Fix the reward, the rest follows.

All numbers come from runs/run_20260512_154221_fresh/metrics.jsonl and two debug episodes rolled out via debug_runner.py at step_005000.pt and step_500000_final.pt. Source code for the analysis lives under /tmp/exp003_4_analysis/.
